paragraphs: Graph neural networks can classify nodes effectively while still having limits on the representations they can learn. This paper asks whether collective inference, a procedure originally intended to improve weaker relational classifiers, can also strengthen these already capable models. The goal is to increase representation power and thereby improve node classification.

The proposed framework, collective learning, adapts collective classification to learning node representations. The authors identify a specific obstacle in earlier combinations of collective inference and graph neural networks: their Monte Carlo sampling was not adapted to representation learning. They show that those earlier approaches consequently fail to increase expressiveness, and design their framework to address that issue.

Experiments combine collective learning with several leading graph neural networks on five real-world network datasets. For inductive node classification in partially labeled graphs, the authors report consistent, significant accuracy improvements across the underlying networks tested. These findings support collective learning as a broadly usable enhancement within that evaluated setting, alongside its contribution to representation power.
icml-2021-a-collective-learning-framewor.tldr: Collective learning adapts collective inference to strengthen GNN representations and improves node classification across five evaluated network datasets.

paragraphs: A bandit learner repeatedly chooses an option while receiving only limited feedback, which may arrive late. This paper studies adversarial losses and modifies Exp3 so that its step size uses information available when each decision is made. Its guarantees adapt to observed delays or losses rather than only their worst possible values.

With suitable tuning, regret scales as the square root of log(K) times (TK + D), where K counts options, T counts rounds, and D totals delays. This is optimal up to logarithmic factors, both in expectation and with high probability. The latter guarantee depends on implicit exploration in loss estimation. A further extension allows unusually delayed rounds to be skipped, trading their count against the remaining delay burden.

An additional AdaGrad-style variant adapts to observed losses and can give much smaller bounds on benign problems. It requires either an advance upper bound on the maximum delay or knowledge of each decision’s delay when choosing. In its bound, delays affect regret only through the best option’s loss.
icml-2021-adapting-to-delays-and-data-in.tldr: Adaptive Exp3 variants obtain regret guarantees that respond to actual feedback delays and losses, with additional delay information required for the loss-adaptive version.

paragraphs: This paper studies decisions that select a group of options at each round, with rewards determined by a known nonlinear function. The setting is adversarial, so the analysis concerns performance under difficult sequences rather than a fixed stochastic reward model. The central question is how much nonlinear rewards change the difficulty of learning.

The authors characterize minimax regret when choosing K out of N options over T rounds. For a polynomial reward of degree d below K, the rate is approximately the square root of N to the power d times T, with logarithmic factors and degree-dependent constants suppressed. When the reward is not a low-degree polynomial, the stated rate instead involves N to the power K, with K-dependent constants.

These results reveal how reward structure can sharply change the dependence on the number of options. The paper also applies the analysis to adversarial assortment optimization in recommendations. In that application’s worst case, an optimal algorithm must treat every possible K-item assortment as independent, showing that shared items alone need not provide useful learning shortcuts.
icml-2021-adversarial-combinatorial-band.tldr: The paper characterizes how nonlinear reward structure can make adversarial subset selection substantially harder, including a worst case requiring independent treatment of every assortment.

paragraphs: In two-player reinforcement learning, an attacker can learn a policy whose behavior causes another agent to perform poorly or react undesirably. Earlier adversarial policy learning relies heavily on the game being zero-sum, meaning that the players’ interests are directly opposed. This paper addresses that dependence by changing what the attacking agent optimizes during learning.

The proposed algorithm resets the optimization goal and introduces a new surrogate objective. That objective provides the learning process with a different target for developing adversarial behavior. The contribution therefore concerns how an adversarial policy is trained through interactions in the game, with the aim of making its exploitation of the target agent more effective.

Experiments report significantly stronger exploitation compared with the existing leading attack. The authors also find that their method can give an agent the ability to take advantage of unfairness in the target game. Finally, retraining agents against these learned adversaries produces stronger resistance to adversarial opponents in the reported experiments, connecting improved attack learning with a potential training benefit.
icml-2021-adversarial-policy-learning-in.tldr: A revised adversarial learning objective produces stronger game-playing attacks and improves resistance when agents are retrained against them.

paragraphs: Self-attention depends on key, query, and value representations, whose design influences how a model uses information. These representations are often customized by hand for particular tasks. AutoAttend treats their design as a search problem, using neural architecture search to find attention representations suited to a downstream task.

The authors construct a search space specifically for attention representations. They then use design knowledge from earlier attention mechanisms to constrain this space, reducing its complexity while preserving its expressivity. This matters because an architecture search must explore useful alternatives without becoming overwhelmed by the number of possible designs.

AutoAttend also introduces context-aware parameter sharing that accounts for characteristics of each candidate sub-architecture. Its purpose is to make architecture estimates more accurate when candidates share parameters during search. Experiments cover eight text classification tasks and four graph node classification tasks, where the authors report improvements over previous leading methods. Together, these results support automated representation design across both language and graph applications in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2021-autoattend-automated-attention.tldr: AutoAttend searches for task-specific attention representations and reports improvements on text and graph node classification tasks.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a target policy would perform using data collected under another policy. A performance estimate alone does not describe its uncertainty. This paper studies how bootstrapping can support statistical inference around fitted Q-evaluation, an evaluation method known to be minimax-optimal in tabular and linear-model settings.

The proposed method uses bootstrapping to infer the distribution of policy evaluation error. The authors prove asymptotic efficiency and distributional consistency for off-policy inference. These are large-sample properties: they establish a theoretical basis for using the bootstrap to characterize evaluation uncertainty as the available data grows, rather than merely producing another estimate of expected performance.

Because repeated bootstrap computations can be expensive, the paper adapts a subsampling procedure that improves runtime by an order of magnitude. Numerical evaluations in classical reinforcement learning environments examine confidence intervals, variance estimation, and correlations between multiple off-policy evaluators. The resulting framework addresses both uncertainty in a single evaluation and statistical relationships among several evaluators.
icml-2021-bootstrapping-fitted-q-evaluat.tldr: Bootstrapping fitted Q-evaluation provides theoretically supported uncertainty estimates, while a subsampling adaptation reduces computational cost.

paragraphs: Maximum likelihood estimates a statistical model by assessing how well it explains observed samples. This paper proposes compressed maximum likelihood, which applies that estimation principle to compressed samples. Its starting point is that the representation supplied to maximum likelihood can itself be part of the statistical method.

The approach is motivated by advances in estimating distribution functionals: properties of a probability distribution that may be the target of inference. This shifts attention toward what needs to be learned from the observations. The proposed framework keeps maximum likelihood as the estimation principle while changing the sample information on which it operates.

The authors establish sample efficiency for several learning tasks over both discrete and continuous domains. These include learning structured densities, estimating probability multisets, and inferring symmetric distribution functionals. The stated contribution is therefore a common estimation approach with sample-efficiency results across several kinds of statistical targets. Its significance lies in showing that applying likelihood to compressed observations can support effective inference for these tasks, rather than requiring the original sample representation throughout.
icml-2021-compressed-maximum-likelihood-.tldr: Compressed maximum likelihood applies likelihood estimation to compressed samples and achieves sample efficiency for several discrete and continuous learning tasks.

paragraphs: An observed link can reflect what someone encountered as well as what they found relevant. In citation networks, for example, researchers may encounter and cite papers from their own fields more often. Training a recommender directly on those links can carry exposure bias into both predictions and evaluation, and repeated recommendations can reinforce that bias.

The paper proposes estimators that use known exposure probabilities to mitigate these effects. Accounting for exposure helps distinguish evidence about relevance from evidence about opportunities to see an item. The authors also introduce a loss function for learning exposure probabilities from data, addressing the need to obtain this information when applying the correction.

Experiments use semi-synthetic data built from real citation networks. In that setting, the methods reliably identify genuinely relevant citations and increase diversity across the recommended papers’ fields of study. These findings connect exposure correction with both relevance and broader recommendations, while the experimental evidence remains specific to the constructed citation-network setting.
icml-2021-correcting-exposure-bias-for-l.tldr: Exposure-aware estimators reduce bias in link recommendations and improve citation relevance and field diversity in semi-synthetic experiments.

paragraphs: Crystallization learning estimates the expected response at a target input without specifying one global regression formula. It uses the geometry of nearby data points to decide where to fit a local linear model. The geometric structure comes from Delaunay simplices, which organize groups of points around the target.

Constructing a Delaunay triangulation across the entire feature space can be computationally difficult, especially in high dimensions. The proposed method instead searches hierarchically for nearby simplices and constructs only the neighborhood needed for the target prediction. This local focus greatly accelerates estimation in the high-dimensional cases considered by the authors.

The simplices’ volumes adapt to the density of the feature data, allowing neighbors to be selected uniformly across directions. The authors argue that this makes the method more robust to local data geometry than existing nonparametric regression methods. They develop asymptotic properties and use synthetic and real-data experiments to demonstrate advantages in estimating conditional expectations and predicting responses.
icml-2021-crystallization-learning-with-.tldr: Crystallization learning builds local Delaunay neighborhoods to make geometrically adaptive regression more computationally practical in high dimensions.

paragraphs: This paper studies actor-critic learning in stochastic games with two players whose objectives are opposed. The actor updates a player’s policy, while the critic supplies value information for that update. The central question is whether a decentralized version of this learning process can converge globally to a minimax equilibrium.

The algorithm operates on a single timescale: each critic update applies the Bellman operator once, and each actor then uses critic information for a policy-gradient update. Each player lacks access to the other player’s actions. This information restriction gives decentralization a concrete meaning and, as the authors describe it, offers a measure of privacy between players.

Both the actor and critic use linear function approximations. For this setting, the authors prove global optimality and sublinear convergence of the generated joint policies to a minimax equilibrium. The result links relatively simple value and policy updates with an equilibrium guarantee despite restricted information. Its scope is the specified zero-sum game setting with linear approximations.
icml-2021-decentralized-single-timescale.tldr: A decentralized actor-critic algorithm with linear approximations is proved to converge to a minimax equilibrium in zero-sum two-player stochastic games.

paragraphs: After a reinforcement learning agent is trained, its performance may deteriorate as its environment changes. This paper develops a way to detect that decline directly from rewards without changing the agent’s policy. It treats an episode as a structured signal, allowing rewards within it to be dependent, differently distributed, and non-Markov.

The authors formulate deterioration as a multivariate change in the mean, potentially with only part of an episode observed. They define the change to match worsening temporal signals and derive a test with optimal statistical power for that detection problem. In control experiments with modified environments, the test detects deteriorated rewards more powerfully than standard tests, often by orders of magnitude.

A bootstrap mechanism called BFAR controls false alarms for episodic signals and enables sequential online testing. The detector operates outside the agent and does not require a learned environment model. This separation makes the approach relevant to monitoring a fixed policy, while its formulation also supports detecting changes in other episodic signals.
icml-2021-detecting-rewards-deterioratio.tldr: An external reward-monitoring test detects episodic performance deterioration and uses bootstrap false-alarm control for online operation.

paragraphs: Calibration concerns whether predicted probabilities agree with observed outcome frequencies. Histogram binning is a popular way to calibrate predictions by grouping them into bins containing similar amounts of data. Despite its practical success, earlier theoretical guarantees covered versions that split the sample to avoid reusing the same observations.

This paper proves distribution-free calibration guarantees for the original method, which does reuse data. The argument exploits a Markov property of order statistics, meaning a particular dependence structure among sorted observations. That structure makes it possible to analyze the reuse directly. A credit-default example shows that the statistical cost of splitting the sample can be practically significant.

The theory also informs recommendations for choosing the number of bins, connecting the guarantees with a concrete implementation decision. In illustrative simulations, the authors introduce validity plots as a calibration assessment tool. They report that these plots convey more information than a single expected calibration error estimate, complementing the theoretical analysis with a richer way to inspect calibration.
icml-2021-distribution-free-calibration-.tldr: The paper proves calibration guarantees for histogram binning with data reuse and develops practical guidance for bin selection and assessment.

paragraphs: Entropy regularization encourages a reinforcement learning policy to keep its action choices varied. This paper extends that idea by incorporating information about actions already represented in the replay buffer. Its aim is more sample-efficient exploration: exploration shaped by the learner’s collected experience as well as its current policy.

The proposed objective maximizes the entropy of a weighted mixture of two distributions. One is the policy’s action distribution, and the other is the sample action distribution obtained from replayed experience. Consequently, the exploration objective depends on both current action choices and the actions present in stored data. This is the central meaning of making entropy regularization sample-aware.

The authors apply policy iteration to this objective to obtain a practical algorithm called diversity actor-critic, or DAC. Numerical results show significant improvements over recent reinforcement learning algorithms. The contribution connects a specific change in the exploration objective with an implementable actor-critic method and reported performance gains, using the replay buffer as a source of information for exploration.
icml-2021-diversity-actor-critic-sample-.tldr: Diversity actor-critic combines policy and replay-buffer action distributions in an entropy objective to improve exploration efficiency.

paragraphs: A text manual can describe how a game works, but an agent must connect its words to what appears in the environment. This paper introduces Messenger, a multitask environment with free-form manuals describing game dynamics. It assumes no predefined mapping between the text and observed entities, so the agent must learn both that mapping and the described behavior.

The proposed model, EMMA, uses attention conditioned on each entity to focus on relevant manual descriptions. It learns an internal grounding between language, entities, and dynamics using only environment rewards. Because the model is differentiable end to end, this grounding is learned as part of the control-learning process.

EMMA successfully generalizes without additional training to unseen games with new dynamics. The authors report a 40% higher win rate than multiple baselines. Nevertheless, its win rate on Messenger’s hardest stage remains 10%. The results therefore demonstrate useful transfer from language while also showing that the most demanding grounding and control problems in this environment remain difficult.
icml-2021-grounding-language-to-entities.tldr: EMMA learns to connect game manuals with entities and dynamics from rewards, enabling zero-shot transfer while struggling on Messenger’s hardest stage.

paragraphs: Small adversarial changes can mislead neural networks, and defenses can themselves be targeted by adaptive attacks. This paper investigates using domain knowledge to improve robustness. Its Knowledge Enhanced Machine Learning Pipeline, KEMLP, combines a main neural network with several weaker auxiliary models whose predictions have meaningful logical relationships.

First-order logic rules express those relationships inside a probabilistic graphical model. For road signs, the relevant knowledge connects sign identity with properties such as shape and content. The auxiliary models therefore contribute related evidence about the main prediction. The authors provide convergence results and prove that KEMLP is more robust than the main network under stated mild conditions.

Experiments on road sign recognition compare the pipeline with adversarial training and other baselines. KEMLP achieves greater robustness across physical attacks, norm-bounded attacks, unforeseen attacks, and natural corruptions, in both white-box and black-box settings, while retaining high clean accuracy. These findings support the use of logically related predictions as an additional source of robustness in the evaluated application.
icml-2021-knowledge-enhanced-machine-lea.tldr: KEMLP combines neural predictions with logical domain knowledge to improve robustness, with conditional theory and road-sign experiments supporting the approach.

paragraphs: Training data often comes from sources that differ in quality and cost. Predicting model performance therefore requires understanding both how much data is available and how it is divided among sources. This paper develops a scaling-law approach that predicts loss as the size and composition of the training dataset change.

The authors turn performance prediction into a learning problem. Using optimal experimental design, they derive a simple rational-function approximation to generalization error that can be fitted from a few model training runs. The purpose is to use those runs to estimate performance across other dataset choices, including configurations beyond the observed training setups.

The approach achieves approximately 0.9 r-squared under substantial extrapolation on two standard supervised learning tasks. It also achieves approximately 0.83 on more challenging machine translation and question answering tasks, where many baselines perform worse than random. These findings support modeling dataset composition explicitly and provide a basis for making more informed data collection decisions when sources have different costs and qualities.
icml-2021-model-performance-scaling-with.tldr: A scaling-law model fitted from a few training runs predicts performance as both training-set size and source composition change.

paragraphs: Alternating minimization is useful in practice for convex and nonconvex optimization, while Nesterov acceleration offers strong theoretical performance for convex problems. This paper combines them in an accelerated alternating minimization algorithm. The aim is to retain the practical structure of alternating updates while obtaining fast convergence guarantees.

For convex problems, the authors prove that the objective error decreases at a rate proportional to 1/k². For nonconvex problems, they establish a 1/k rate for the squared gradient norm, where k counts iterations. These measures describe different achievements: objective accuracy in the convex case and progress toward stationarity in the nonconvex case. The algorithm requires neither prior knowledge of convexity nor smoothness parameters such as a gradient Lipschitz constant.

The authors characterize the method as uniformly optimal for smooth convex and nonconvex problems. They also develop a primal-dual version for strongly convex problems with linear constraints. That extension achieves 1/k² rates for both the primal objective residual and constraint feasibility, addressing solution quality and satisfaction of the constraints together.
icml-2021-on-a-combination-of-alternatin.tldr: Accelerated alternating minimization achieves convex and nonconvex convergence guarantees without requiring prior knowledge of convexity or smoothness parameters.

paragraphs: For complex objects such as text, images, or genomes, available interventions may act indirectly. A writing program changes text through a broader process, just as a gene therapy can affect genetic material without providing isolated control over every component. This paper formalizes causal response estimation when these broader, crude interventions are the available actions.

Given a collection of candidate mediators, the authors propose a two-step method for predicting the causal responses to crude interventions. They also develop a testing procedure for identifying mediators of those interventions. These two components address related questions: what effect an intervention will have, and which candidate variables mediate its influence.

The approach is evaluated on simulated and real-world-inspired examples. Those demonstrations show efficient estimation of intervention effects using limited data from new treatment regimes. The contribution is presented as an initial solution to a practical causal problem: estimating the consequences of actions that operate on complex objects without assuming access to fine-grained interventions on their individual components.
icml-2021-operationalizing-complex-cause.tldr: The paper formalizes causal estimation for indirect interventions on complex objects and proposes methods to predict their effects and identify mediators.

paragraphs: In parametric Bayesian learning, an unknown parameter determines the data distribution and has a prior distribution. Minimum excess risk measures the difference between the best expected loss achievable from training data and the best achievable if that parameter were directly observed. This paper studies that gap through information theory.

The authors formulate the problem as constrained rate-distortion optimization, connecting available information with achievable prediction accuracy. They bound it using two simpler rate-distortion functions. The lower bound allows any process using R bits of information from the parameter. The upper bound imposes the further restriction that the R bits must come through the training set.

This distinction separates information about the underlying parameter from information accessible through observations. The authors bound the difference between the two constructions and show that they can produce order-wise tight rates for minimum excess risk under certain conditions. The upper construction also connects the analysis with information-theoretic bounds on the generalization gap in frequentist learning, linking two perspectives on statistical learning.
icml-2021-rate-distortion-analysis-of-mi.tldr: A rate-distortion formulation bounds the extra prediction loss caused by learning an unknown Bayesian parameter from data.

paragraphs: Online learning becomes particularly difficult when objectives are nonconvex and nonsmooth, decisions are constrained, and gradient information is noisy. In the setting studied here, first-order methods cannot achieve the usual external-regret objective. The paper instead develops a local-regret criterion based on nonconvex optimality measures.

Its criterion uses a proximal-gradient mapping, allowing local regret to account for the constraints and nonsmooth structure of the problem. It also includes an earlier local-regret definition as a special case. The authors develop a method using stochastic first-order feedback and a simpler alternative for exact first-order feedback, both designed to achieve no local regret.

Both methods are order-optimal in the minimax sense, and the paper bounds the number of proximal-gradient queries they require. The analysis also connects online learning with offline stochastic nonconvex optimization. This yields a new proximal-gradient scheme with complexity guarantees matching those obtained through variance-reduction techniques. The guarantees concern the proposed local criterion rather than a claim of globally minimizing arbitrary nonconvex objectives.
icml-2021-regret-minimization-in-stochas.tldr: A proximal-gradient definition of local regret enables order-optimal learning guarantees for constrained, nonsmooth, nonconvex problems with stochastic feedback.

paragraphs: Neural image compression must train through quantization, the step that converts representations into discrete values. Differentiable approximations make training possible, but they introduce tradeoffs. Additive uniform noise creates a mismatch between training and testing, while the paper finds that straight-through estimation and soft-to-hard annealing weaken latent representations and hurt the balance between bitrate and distortion.

The proposed soft-then-hard strategy separates learning an expressive latent space from closing that mismatch. Training first uses a soft approach to develop the representation, then introduces hard quantization. The motivation is to retain representation quality while bringing the learned compression system into alignment with the quantization used when it operates.

The authors also use scaled additive uniform noise to adapt the quantization granularity beyond fixed integer quantization. A newly derived variational upper bound on the actual rate supports this extension. Experiments report stable training, ease of adoption, and strong effectiveness, especially for complex compression models. These findings connect the training procedure with both representation quality and control over compression granularity.
icml-2021-soft-then-hard-rethinking-the-.tldr: Soft-then-hard quantization first learns expressive image representations and then removes the training–testing mismatch, with an extension for adaptive quantization granularity.

paragraphs: Batch reinforcement learning uses previously collected data to evaluate or improve a policy. When many candidate features are available but only some are relevant, sparse linear approximations can reduce the statistical burden. This paper analyzes how sparsity affects both off-policy evaluation and policy optimization in high-dimensional settings.

For evaluation, the authors establish a finite-sample error bound for Lasso fitted Q-evaluation with no polynomial dependence on the full feature dimension. They then reduce Lasso bias by selecting features with group Lasso and evaluating on the selected set. Under an additional signal-strength assumption, a sharper bound accounts for mismatch between the data distribution and the target policy’s occupancy measure.

For optimization, the Lasso fitted Q-iteration bound depends on the number of relevant features and a restricted eigenvalue of the data covariance. Nearly matching minimax lower bounds complement the upper bounds. Together, the results show why feature sparsity can improve sample efficiency while emphasizing that the collected data must also be well conditioned for effective sparse policy learning.
icml-2021-sparse-feature-selection-makes.tldr: Sparse feature methods improve theoretical sample efficiency in batch reinforcement learning, with guarantees shaped by signal strength, distribution mismatch, and data conditioning.

paragraphs: Several properties of stochastic gradient descent have been associated with generalization: the flatness of a solution, the ratio of step size to batch size, and the heaviness of the distribution’s tails for learned weights. This paper argues that these perspectives are linked through the behavior of SGD’s iterates.

The central claim is conditional: depending on loss curvature and algorithm parameters, the iterates can converge to a heavy-tailed stationary distribution. The authors rigorously establish this phenomenon for quadratic optimization. Even linear regression with independent, identically distributed data having finite moments of every order can produce iterates with heavy tails and infinite variance. Thus, heavy-tailed iterates need not originate in heavy-tailed observations.

The analysis characterizes how tail behavior varies with step size, batch size, dimension, and curvature. The authors then draw insights for deep learning and support their theory with synthetic experiments and fully connected and convolutional networks. The rigorous quadratic results provide a mechanism connecting these quantities, while the neural-network experiments explore its relevance beyond that theoretical setting.
icml-2021-the-heavy-tail-phenomenon-in-s.tldr: SGD can generate heavy-tailed iterates even from well-behaved data, linking tail behavior to curvature, step size, and batch size.

paragraphs: Cooperative reinforcement learning requires agents to discover actions that work well together. VDN and QMIX make decentralized decisions convenient by expressing a centralized action value through monotonic combinations of individual utilities. However, that restriction can prevent them from solving tasks that demand substantial coordination at the same timestep.

This paper shows that improving joint exploration during training can overcome this problem. Its method, Universal Value Exploration, or UneVEn, learns several related tasks simultaneously using a linear decomposition of universal successor features. Policies from related tasks that have already been solved then help guide the agents’ joint exploration toward better coordination.

The authors evaluate UneVEn on exploration games, cooperative predator-prey tasks requiring significant coordination, and StarCraft II micromanagement benchmarks. They report that it solves tasks where other leading multi-agent methods fail. The findings highlight training-time exploration as a way to address coordination difficulties associated with restricted joint value functions, using progress on related tasks to help agents discover effective collective behavior.
icml-2021-uneven-universal-value-explora.tldr: UneVEn uses policies learned on related tasks to improve joint exploration and solve demanding cooperative coordination problems.

paragraphs: Instrumental variables can help estimate causal effects despite unobserved confounding. Their use typically relies on an exclusion assumption: an instrument affects the response only through the treatment. This paper develops consistent estimation when some candidate instruments violate that assumption, provided there is suitable agreement among the valid candidates.

A majority of candidates being valid is sufficient; more generally, the modal candidate-response relationship must be valid. The method estimates the modal prediction from an ensemble of instrumental-variable estimators. It is compatible with different underlying estimators, provided each valid instrument independently identifies the treatment effect. These conditions are essential to the stated guarantee.

The ensemble approach can also use machine-learning estimators for conditional average treatment effects on complex, high-dimensional data. Experiments with deep-network estimators produce accurate estimates, including in a challenging simulated Mendelian randomization problem. The contribution makes it possible to use a collection containing invalid instruments under the stated validity structure, while retaining flexibility in how each individual causal estimate is produced.
icml-2021-valid-causal-inference-with-so.tldr: An ensemble’s modal prediction supports consistent causal estimation with some invalid instruments when the valid instruments satisfy the stated identification and agreement conditions.
